newsitem.title: JAPAN: Markets unshaken by latest Sumitomo bombshell.
newsitem.headline: Markets unshaken by latest Sumitomo bombshell.

text.p: Financial and commodity markets were unshaken on Friday by Sumitomo Corp's latest bombshell -- that it had lost $2.6 billion from unauthorised copper trades, $800 million more than its original estimate.
Prices of copper and of Sumitomo shares showed only modest reaction to the news, in sharp contrast to the collapse in both after Sumitomo's June 13 announcement of a $1.8 billion loss.
"The market isn't moving at all," said a copper trader at one of Japan's leading trade houses.
Nomura Research Institute said on Friday that the stock market had been well aware of the possibility that Sumitomo's loss from the trading scandal could be bigger than the initial estimate.

On Friday, Sumitomo Bank Ltd reiterated its pledge, first extended in June, of full financial support to Sumitomo Corp, while Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry said it saw no reason to intervene in the case.

"The trading loss is quite big and Sumitomo management will take appropriate action following the loss," Trade Minister Shunpei Tsukahara told a news conference. "This is a matter of a private company so I would hesitate to intervene."

Sumitomo announced it had revised upward its estimated copper market losses after Thursday's stock market close. It blamed the losses on more than a decade of unauthorised trades by dismissed copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
It said it had now liquidated most of the unauthorised copper positions and expected no further revisions of its loss estimates.
The company also accused Hamanaka of forgery and breach of trust and said it planned to press criminal charges against him.
A source in the prosecutor's office said the Tokyo District Public Prosecutor's Office had already begun probing the case and questioning Sumitomo officials.
But while Japan's legal machinery appears finally to be lurching into action on the case, the markets have largely lost interest.

Prices of world-benchmark copper on the London Metal Exchange managed a brief, modest rally to two-week highs after Sumitomo's announcement, amid relief that Hamanaka's positions were largely liquidated, but then retraced to a modestly higher close at $1,936 a tonne, up $11.

The stock market also reacted calmly to the news, with Sumitomo shares slipping to 905 yen in early trade, still above a low of 890 hit two weeks ago, and then bouncing back to a close of 925, off 14.

In the overall stock market, players were more influenced by uncertainty about a possible general election next month and the prospects for a supplementary budget, brokers said. The closely watched 225-issue Nikkei Average closed down 210.61 points, or 0.99 percent, at 21,112.24.

Friday's measured reactions were in marked contrast to the first day of trading after the June 13 announcement, when Sumitomo's share price fell by the 200-yen daily limit and LME copper prices began an eight-session tumble of nearly 20 percent, to a two-and-a-half-year low of $1,745 a tonne.
"With this (Thursday's announcement), there should be no more strange moves in the copper market," the copper trader said.
